name: Apple CloudKit
tagline: Apple's iCloud record store for apps: private per-user data, a public database and built-in sync.
description: CloudKit is the backend Apple runs inside iCloud for third-party apps. Each app gets a container with a public database, a private database per iCloud user and a shared database for records shared through CKShare; data is organised as typed records in zones, with subscriptions that push changes to devices. Private data counts against the user's own iCloud storage rather than the developer's bill, which is why so many indie and Apple-platform apps use it as their only backend. Core Data and SwiftData can mirror into it automatically, and CKSyncEngine (iOS 17, 2023) handles the hard parts of incremental sync for custom stores. The catch is reach: it is tied to Apple IDs and Apple platforms, with only CloudKit JS and web services for the browser, and querying is far simpler than a general database.

pricing.notes: Free for developers within generous public-database and request limits that grow with active users; each user's private data counts against their own iCloud storage plan.

scale.notes: Private data scales with the user base because it lives in each user's iCloud account; Apple advertises up to 1 PB for the public database. Apple does not document regional placement or replication.

strengths: Private data is stored in each user's iCloud quota, so per-user storage costs the developer nothing
No sign-up flow: users are already authenticated with their Apple ID
Core Data and SwiftData sync to it with NSPersistentCloudKitContainer and almost no code
CKSyncEngine (iOS 17+) manages change tokens, batching and retries for custom sync
Sharing between users is built in through CKShare and the share sheet
Encrypted fields in the private database for sensitive data
weaknesses: Only works for users with an Apple ID; Android and other platforms are second-class
Simple predicate queries only: no joins, aggregates or server-side logic
Schema must be promoted from development to production in the CloudKit Console
You cannot export or self-host it; migrating off means rebuilding sync elsewhere
useCases: Syncing app data across a user's iPhone, iPad and Mac
Indie and Apple-only apps that want a backend without servers
Collaborative documents and lists shared between iCloud users
Core Data or SwiftData apps that need cloud backup and sync
notIdealFor: Cross-platform apps with Android or web-first users
Server-side workloads that need a general-purpose database
